Configuration reference

Copperline is configured by a TOML file: the file passed with --config, else ./copperline.toml if present, else a copperline.toml beside the Copperline executable, else the configuration saved with the configuration screen’s Save default button (see The window, status bar, and menus). Every field is optional; missing fields use the defaults documented here. copperline.example.toml in the repository root is a commented companion to this reference.

A copperline.toml in the working directory or beside the executable describes a machine to run: like --config, it skips the configuration screen, and the machine starts running at once (unless the file sets [emulation] power_on = false). The copy beside the executable works whatever directory Copperline is started from, so an installation can carry its own default machine. For a downloaded .AppImage, put it beside the .AppImage file. On macOS, put it beside Copperline.app; a copy inside the bundle’s Contents/MacOS folder also works, but the one beside the bundle wins. macOS runs a downloaded app that has not been moved out of its download folder from a temporary private copy, which cannot see the files beside it. Move Copperline.app with the Finder (to Applications, say) before relying on a file beside it. Relative paths inside it work as in any configuration file: a media path such as rom = "KICK31.ROM" that is not in the working directory is looked for in the matching media folder (see Relative media paths), so a ROM kept in ~/Documents/Copperline/roms is found whatever directory Copperline was started from.

--factory ignores the saved default and a copperline.toml beside the executable, and starts from Copperline’s own settings. It also leaves the CDTV’s default bookmark RAM file alone (see [cd] below). --config and ./copperline.toml always win over it anyway. With neither default present, the flag changes nothing.

Settings changed from the menu during a session that started without --config, a copperline.toml or --factory are written into the saved default as they change (only the changed keys; see Settings the menu remembers).

If the saved default cannot be read or parsed, Copperline logs a warning and continues with built-in settings and any command-line overrides. It leaves the saved file untouched. A saved default that parses but no longer validates -- a disk image that moved, a drive not yet mounted -- opens the configuration screen on the built-in settings with the reason on its status line, so it can be fixed before Save default replaces it. Errors in --config or a copperline.toml still report the requested configuration problem.

Configuration parsing rejects unknown keys, invalid CPU or chipset names, and out-of-range sizes. Media are opened during startup; depending on the device, an unavailable image either stops startup or leaves the unit absent with a warning in the log.

For older key spellings and unknown field errors, see configuration compatibility and the changelog. Match the manual version to the executable before copying a configuration.

Paths on Windows¶

This applies to every path field below (rom, disk images, hard-drive files, the SCSI ROMs, and so on). In a TOML double-quoted string the backslash is an escape character, so a Windows path written the obvious way (rom = "C:\Kickstarts\KICK31.ROM") is rejected: \K is not a valid escape. Use any one of:

rom = 'C:\Kickstarts\KICK31.ROM'    # single quotes: a literal string, no escaping
rom = "C:\\Kickstarts\\KICK31.ROM"  # double quotes: backslashes doubled
rom = "C:/Kickstarts/KICK31.ROM"    # forward slashes also work on Windows

Single-quoted literal strings are the least error-prone. macOS and Linux paths use forward slashes and need none of this. TOML paths do not expand ~ or shell variables; use an absolute path or a relative one (see below).

Relative media paths¶

A relative path is looked for in the working directory first. A ROM, disk or CD path that is not there is then looked for in the matching media folder from [paths]. By default these are under the host data directory, so rom = "KICK31.ROM" finds ~/Documents/Copperline/roms/KICK31.ROM and [copperhf] unit0 = "Workbench.hdf" finds ~/Documents/Copperline/harddrives/Workbench.hdf, whichever directory Copperline was started from. That matters for a copy started from the Dock, the Start menu or a desktop launcher, whose working directory is rarely one you chose.

PathsMedia folder
rom, extended_rom, fmv_rom, [scsi] rom/rom_odd, [lide] rom/rom_bank2, [sf2000sd] rom, [cartridge] romroms
[serial] mt32_control_rom, mt32_pcm_romroms/mt32, then roms
[floppy.dfN] imagesfloppies
[ide], [scsi], [lide], [copperhf] and [sf2000sd] drivesharddrives, then cds
[[filesys]] folders, a [pcmcia] CF cardharddrives
[cd] imagecds

A path with folders in it is looked up the same way (rom = "kickstarts/KICK31.ROM" finds roms/kickstarts/KICK31.ROM). A media folder that does not exist is skipped; none is created. A path found in neither place is reported as written. Absolute paths are always used as they are, and every other relative path in a configuration (bezel stickers, shaders, printer output, battery-RAM files and so on) is still relative to the working directory. Paths given to scheduled input such as --insert-disk-after are also used as written.

Command-line overrides¶

Long options taking a value accept either --flag VALUE or --flag=VALUE, including --config=machine.toml and --script=input.clscript. For an option with several arguments, the inline value is its first argument: --screenshot-after=10 out.png or --window-position=-40 75. Values keep any further = characters. Switches such as --factory and --noaudio take no value; --noaudio=false is an error.

--help (or -h) and --version (or -V) print to stdout and exit successfully; -c is short for --config. Invalid arguments print to stderr and exit with status 1. A mistyped long option suggests a close, unambiguous match when one is available.

The most common machine knobs can be set on the command line without writing a config file. These flags layer on top of the config file (or, when there is none, the built-in defaults) and are validated by exactly the same parsers and range checks as the equivalent TOML fields:

For example, to boot a stock A1200 profile but with 8 MB of fast RAM and a faster CPU, with no config file at all:

./target/release/copperline --model A1200 --fast 8M --cpu-clock 28 KICK31.ROM

A --model profile supplies the chipset, CPU, and memory defaults of a real machine; the other flags then override individual values on top of it, just as explicit [cpu]/[chipset]/[memory] sections override a [machine] profile in a config file.

The serial and parallel ports have further per-run flags -- --midi-in, --midi-out, --mt32-control-rom, --mt32-pcm-rom, --mt32-panel, --sampler-audio-input, and --sampler-input-gain -- described with their [serial] and [parallel] keys below. Non-configuration setup and session flags (such as --run, --calibrate-gamepad, --install-net-helper, --profile-live-audio, and the --netplay-* options) are covered in copperline --help and their matching guide chapters.

Top level¶

rom = "KICK13.ROM"            # Kickstart image, 512 KiB (or a 256 KiB 1.x part)
extended_rom = "cd32ext.rom"  # optional: CDTV (256K at $F00000) or
                              # CD32 (512K at $E00000) extended ROM
# fmv = true                  # CD32: fit the FMV module (bundled open ROM)
# fmv_rom = "another.rom"     # CD32: fit the FMV module with this ROM
# identify = false            # drop the Copperline identification board
                              # from the Zorro chain (default: present)

identify controls a small, inert Zorro autoconfig board Copperline puts on the expansion chain (manufacturer 5192 / product 2) so guest software such as identify.library can detect that it is running under the emulator. It is on by default and does not change the machine’s usable memory; set identify = false for a chain with no emulator-identifying board. See Writing Zorro board plugins for details.

A positional ROM argument on the command line overrides rom. Positional media and .toml configurations are also accepted; see Opening files. Omit rom entirely (and pass no ROM argument) to boot the bundled AROS open-source Kickstart replacement, Copperline’s default boot ROM; its main and extended halves are found as described under Where bundled files are found. The menu’s Load Kickstart ROM... item fits a different ROM at runtime and hard-resets the machine. Machine profiles that need an extended ROM (CDTV, CD32) will tell you if it is missing.

The Kickstart and extended-ROM keys accept images in either byte order. Besides plain CPU-order dumps, Copperline recognizes the byte-swapped images prepared for EPROM programmers from their header and restores them on load, so either file boots identically. (The single-chip .bin ROM files in Hyperion’s Kickstart 3.1.4/3.2 releases, such as kick.a500a600a2000.46.143.bin, are of this kind: every 16-bit word has its bytes exchanged.) A 256 KiB Kickstart 1.x part is mirrored across the 512 KiB ROM window, as it decodes on real hardware. The split hi/lo chip pairs for the 32-bit machines are not accepted; use the matching single-file image instead.

fmv = true fits the CD32 Full Motion Video module with Copperline’s bundled open-source 256 KiB replacement ROM, and fmv_rom = "path" fits it with a custom image (such as the Commodore v40.30 ROM) instead; both are valid only with the CD32 machine profile. The cartridge slot is empty by default: a stock CD32 has no module, and fitting one changes the guest’s memory layout and boot timing enough to alter titles that never used it (fmv_rom = "", the older spelling of an empty slot, is still accepted). The module autoconfigures ahead of the standard Zorro chain, driving the CL450 video and L64111 MPEG Layer II audio decoders through guest code. The launcher’s ROM tab exposes this setting as FMV module ROM.

The open ROM includes a clean-room cd32mpeg.device and videocd.library compatible with CD32 Kickstart 3.1. The library identifies inserted Video CDs and parses their metadata. Under CD32 Kickstart, the bundled version 41 cdstrap autoboots Video CDs into a track menu: Up/Down navigates, Red plays, and Blue stops or exits. Standard CD32 game discs pass through to the default boot sequence. The bundled AROS ROM has its own MPEG device and CDXL playback support but bypasses cartridge diagnostics, so the cartridge’s library and player currently work only under Kickstart. Neither path needs proprietary Commodore code or CL450 microcode: Copperline models the CL450 command interface at the host level.

Copperline also names the ROM it is given. A ROM file’s name is whatever its dumper called it, so the image is identified by checksum against a table of the released Amiga boot ROMs -- every Kickstart from 1.0 to 3.2.3, the CD32 Kickstart and extended ROM, the CDTV/A570 extended ROMs and the A1000 bootstrap -- and the version is reported as, for example, Kickstart 3.1 (40.68) A1200. Identification survives the same forms the loader accepts (byte-swapped dumps, a 256 KiB part stored doubled), and an Amiga Forever image still in its AMIROMTYPE1 container is reported as encrypted rather than unknown. The identification appears in the start-up config: log line, in the About window’s ROM: line, in the OSD when a ROM is fitted from the menu, and under each path row of the machine-configuration screen’s ROM tab. The bundled AROS ROM reports itself as bundled AROS; any other image the table does not carry -- DiagROM, a ROM you built yourself -- goes unnamed and boots as usual.

Where bundled files are found¶

Copperline ships the open files it fits by default -- the AROS boot ROM, the open CD32 FMV, A2091, A4091, and lide boot ROMs, and the HRTMon cartridge image -- together with the WHDLoad support archives (release builds include them; otherwise fetch them once with tools/fetch-whdload.sh or Download on the launcher’s WHDLoad page). Each set lives in its own subdirectory, looked for in this order:

  1. the directory named by the set’s environment variable (below);

  2. <sub>/ beside the executable;

  3. Contents/Resources/<sub>/ in a macOS .app bundle;

  4. ../share/copperline/<sub>/ relative to the executable (a Homebrew or Unix install);

  5. assets/<sub>/ in the source tree, for a development build.

The WHDLoad archives are also looked for in whdload/support/ under the host data directory (where the launcher downloads them), ahead of the source tree.

Files<sub>Override
AROS boot ROM (aros-amiga-m68k-rom.bin, aros-amiga-m68k-ext.bin)arosCOPPERLINE_AROS_DIR
CD32 FMV module ROM (copperline-fmv.rom)fmvCOPPERLINE_FMV_DIR
HRTMon cartridge image (hrtmon.rom)hrtmonCOPPERLINE_HRTMON_DIR
A2091 boot ROM (copperline-a2091.rom)a2091COPPERLINE_A2091_DIR
A4091 boot ROM (a4091_cdfs.rom)a4091COPPERLINE_A4091_DIR
lide boot ROMs (lide.rom, lide-atbus.rom, cdfs.rom)lideCOPPERLINE_LIDE_DIR
WHDLoad support archives (WHDLoad_usr.lha, skick346.lha)whdbootCOPPERLINE_WHDBOOT_DIR

A key that names its own file (rom, fmv_rom, [scsi] rom, [lide] rom, [cartridge] rom, [whdload] whd_package / skick_package) is used instead of the search.

[paths] -- where files go¶

[paths]
# base = "/somewhere/else"   # move the whole tree; the rest are under it
# states = "states"          # save states, incl. the quick-save slots
# screenshots = "screenshots"
# recordings = "recordings"  # video captures, GIF clips and recorded input scripts
# nvram = "nvram"            # battery-backed RAMs, incl. CD32 game saves
# traces = "traces"          # debugger traces and waveform captures
# configs = "configs"        # configurations saved from the launcher
# roms = "roms"              # the rest are media folders (see below):
# mt32_roms = "roms/mt32"    # MT-32 control and PCM ROMs (default: mt32 inside roms)
# floppies = "floppies"
# harddrives = "harddrives"
# cds = "cds"

[paths] sets where Copperline writes its output files, where file dialogs open when their field is empty (until a dialog for that kind of file has been used in the session -- from then on it opens where the last one was answered), and where a relative media path is looked for when the working directory does not have it (see Relative media paths). Every key is optional and falls back to the default directory structure under the host data directory (~/Documents/Copperline on macOS and Linux, %USERPROFILE%\Documents\Copperline on Windows, or the application folder in a portable installation).

Relative paths are resolved against base (which itself defaults to the host data directory), while absolute paths are used directly. Output folders are created automatically on first write. Media folders are not created automatically and are only used when they exist.

These name folders on the machine that runs the configuration, so a config copied to another machine may name folders that are not there. At startup each entry set here is checked and one that cannot be found is ignored with a warning in the log, falling back to its default -- the check waits no more than a moment, so a dead network mount delays starting rather than preventing it. Explicit output paths on the command line (--screenshot-after, --save-state-after, and so on) are used exactly as written and never consult this section.

[machine] -- machine profiles¶

[machine]
profile = "A1200" # A1000, A500, A500OCS, A500Plus (A500+), A2000, A600, A1200, A3000, A4000, CDTV, CD32
rtc = true        # add a battery RTC (default: only A500+/A2000/CDTV/A3000/A4000 ship with one)
# rtc_chip = "RP5C01"              # MSM6242 (default) or RP5C01 (A3000/A4000 default)
# rtc_time = "2005-03-18 01:58:29" # seed the clock; it then ticks in emulated time
# rtc_frozen = true                # stop the seeded clock at rtc_time exactly
# battmem = "battmem.nvram"        # RP5C01 battery-RAM backing file (default when fitted: in the [paths] nvram folder)
# mem_controller = "ramsey-07"     # none, ramsey-04 (A3000), ramsey-07 (A4000)
# rom_scsi_device_disable = true   # skip the ROM's scsi.device (default: when its bus has no drives)

A machine profile bundles the chipset, CPU, memory, gate array, and peripheral defaults of a real machine. The key is profile (the deprecated model alias still parses) so that it never collides with [cpu] model. Explicit [cpu], [chipset], and [memory] sections override individual profile defaults. Without a [machine] section you get the A500 Rev 6A default (the same as the A500 profile: ECS 8372A Agnus, OCS 8362 Denise, 68000, 512K chip RAM, 512K trapdoor slow RAM) -- the most common and most-targeted Amiga. An explicit [chipset] revision overrides the per-machine chips, so revision = "OCS" gives a plain 8371/8362 OCS machine.

rtc exists because most Amigas shipped without a battery-backed clock. The A500Plus (an OKI RTC soldered to the Rev 8A board), A2000, CDTV, A3000, and A4000 fit one by default; the base A500/A500OCS, A600, A1200, A1000, and CD32 have none. Set rtc = true to add one -- for an A600HD or a clock-equipped A1200, say -- so the Workbench clock keeps time.

rtc_chip names the part in that socket, because Commodore used two with different register protocols: the OKI MSM6242 on the small boxes, the A2000, the CDTV, and the aftermarket clock expansions, and the Ricoh RP5C01 on the A3000/A4000 motherboards (the Ricoh also carries 26 nibbles of battery RAM, which AmigaOS uses via battmem.resource on those machines). The default follows the profile -- RP5C01 on A3000/A4000, MSM6242 everywhere else -- and setting the key implies rtc = true. AmigaOS probes for either part, so the choice is mostly invisible to it, but Linux/m68k does not probe: it drives the chip the machine model dictates, so an A3000/A4000 booting Linux needs the RP5C01 answering for its clock to work.

battmem persists the RP5C01’s battery-backed registers -- the 26 RAM nibbles behind battmem.resource plus the alarm and 12/24 settings -- across runs, the way the real board’s battery does. This is where scsi.device keeps its per-unit SCSI host settings (an A3000’s or A4091’s synchronous-transfer, disconnect, and last-drive options, including remembering attached CD-ROM drives), so without it those revert every run. The file uses the same .nvram layout as WinUAE and Amiberry, so backing files interchange between emulators; only the battery payload loads back -- the time-of-save digits in the file never override the (host- or rtc_time-driven) clock. Whenever an RP5C01 is fitted it defaults to battmem.nvram in the [paths] nvram folder (a battmem.nvram already in the working directory from an earlier Copperline keeps being used from there); point it elsewhere with a path, or set battmem = "" to keep the battery registers session-only. A persisted file carries guest-visible state from one run into the next by design, so delete or disable it where byte-for-byte reproducible headless runs matter.

rtc_time seeds the clock instead of letting it mirror the host’s: the value is either an integer (Unix seconds, UTC) or a string "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:SS]" giving exactly the wall-clock time the guest reads at power-on. A seeded clock ticks with emulated time, so the time the guest sees is deterministic and reproducible byte-for-byte across runs -- the way to test time-dependent guest software (TOTP/RFC 6238 vectors, timestamped logs, date rollovers) or just to boot into a fixed date. Setting a time implies rtc = true; combining it with an explicit rtc = false is an error. rtc_frozen = true additionally stops the tick so every read returns rtc_time exactly. Both are also available as --rtc-time / --rtc-frozen CLI flags, and a control-protocol session can inspect and move the clock live with rtc.get / rtc.set (see the control protocol).

Two guest-side notes: Kickstart 2.0+ loads the system time from the battery clock automatically at boot, while Kickstart 1.3 only does so when the startup-sequence runs SetClock LOAD; and the chip’s two-digit year registers mean AmigaOS applies its usual century window, so seeds outside 1978-2077 will not read back as the year you set. A host-initiated reset or power cycle restarts the emulated timeline and therefore restarts a seeded clock from rtc_time; a guest-initiated reboot (the 68000 RESET instruction) leaves it ticking, like real battery-backed hardware.

The guest can set the clock: the chip’s counters are read/write, so SetClock SAVE (or the Time preferences editor, or another OS’s hwclock) takes effect and the clock counts on from the written time. That time belongs to the running machine: it counts on through a guest reboot and a keyboard reset, and travels in save states, but the host clock is never changed, and the next power cycle starts again from the host time or from rtc_time.

The A3000 and A4000 profiles are the big-box machines. They carry a Ramsey memory controller (mem_controller), whose two registers answer at $DE0003 and $DE0043, and Gary rather than Gayle -- so no PCMCIA slot and no Gayle IDE.

  • The A3000 has its motherboard SCSI: a Super DMAC at $DD0000 driving a WD33C93, which Kickstart’s own scsi.device initializes at boot. Attach drives to it with [scsi] controller = "a3000" (the default controller on an A3000; see the [scsi] section below).

  • The A4000 has its motherboard IDE interface at $DD2020; attach drives with [ide], exactly as on a Gayle machine.

rom_scsi_device_disable skips Kickstart’s built-in disk driver. It defaults on when the machine’s own controller -- the IDE port of an A600, A1200, or A4000, or the A3000’s SCSI -- has no drives configured: with nothing to boot, the driver only costs startup time probing an empty bus. Configuring a drive turns the driver back on automatically (it is the boot path for those drives), and setting the flag explicitly wins in either direction. The ROM file itself is never modified.

Both profiles fit their stock 4M of Ramsey-controlled motherboard fast RAM; [memory] motherboard resizes it up to 16M, and on the A4000 up to 64M via the motherboard RAM expansion space (see the [memory] section). [memory] accelerator adds CPU-slot RAM at $08000000 on any 32-bit machine.

mem_controller is normally left to the profile. It is a separate key because Ramsey’s registers collide with nothing else, so it can be fitted to a wedge machine to exercise diagnostic tools that expect one.

The A1000 profile models the original Amiga, which has no Kickstart ROM. Its rom is instead the 64K bootstrap ROM (“Amiga ROM Bootstrap”); on power-up the bootstrap loads Kickstart from the Kickstart disk in DF0 into 256K of writable control store (WCS) at $FC0000, write-protects it, and runs it, as the real machine does. So an A1000 config names the bootstrap ROM as rom and puts the Kickstart disk in [floppy.df0]; leave it in and the machine boots to Kickstart (which then asks for a Workbench disk). See the ready-made a1000.example.toml.

The A500 profile models the common Rev 6A board: the ECS “Fatter” 8372A Agnus (a 1 MiB chip-RAM reach and the software-selectable PAL/NTSC switch via BEAMCON0) paired with the original OCS 8362 Denise. It is therefore an Agnus-only ECS upgrade, not a full-ECS machine -- the OCS Denise means no superhires or BRDRBLNK, as on the real board. Chip RAM defaults to the stock 512K but accepts up to 1M ([memory] chip = "1M"); more than 1M is rejected because the 8372A cannot address it. Booting with no [machine] section uses the same Rev 6A defaults; select A500OCS or set [chipset] revision = "OCS" for the older 8371/8362 machine.

The A2000 profile models the B2000 Rev 6.x motherboard, the revision most A2000s are: the same chip pair as the A500 Rev 6A (the 8372A Agnus with the OCS 8362 Denise), a 68000 at 7.09 MHz, the board’s 1 MiB of soldered RAM all addressed as chip RAM, nothing at $C00000, and the battery-backed OKI MSM6242 clock on the motherboard. Its Gary is the A500’s part, so the motherboard address decode is the A500’s. The board’s five Zorro II slots are the autoconfig chain every profile has: [memory] fast, [scsi] (an A2091 makes it an A2000HD), [[zorro]] and the other Zorro II boards configure on it with no further setup. There is no slot count to configure and none is enforced. The other board revisions are overrides on the same profile:

BoardSettings on top of profile = "A2000"
Rev 4.x (8371 Fat Agnus, 512K chip plus 512K at $C00000)[chipset] revision = "OCS", [memory] chip = "512K", slow = "512K"
Rev 6.x (the default)none
Late Rev 6 with the ECS Denise[chipset] revision = "ECS" (or denise = "ECS")
With an accelerator in the CPU slot[cpu] model, plus [memory] accelerator for its RAM

revision = "OCS" on its own is refused, because the 8371 cannot address the Rev 6.x board’s megabyte as chip RAM. The original German A2000-A (an A1000-derived design without Gary) is not modelled. The profile boots the bundled AROS ROM like every other, and Commodore’s A500/A2000 Kickstarts (1.2, 1.3, 2.0x and 3.1) as the A500 profile does.

[emulation]¶

[emulation]
power_on = true            # false = start powered off at the test screen
auto_launch = false        # true = the launcher runs this file at once
pacing_budget = "cycles"   # "cycles" (hardware-accurate) or "instructions"
realtime_priority = false  # true = raise the pacer/audio thread priority
warp_speed = "max"         # turbo limit: "2x", "4x", "8x", "16x", or "max"
warp_boot = false          # warp the boot until storage goes idle
warp_boot_idle = 10        # ...for this many emulated seconds
# warp_until = 12.0        # or warp until an absolute emulated time
uaelib = true              # uaelib trap and WinUAE memory-write debug output
uaelib_files = false       # opt-in file helpers, below the --run directory
rewind = false             # true = record rewind history from power-on
rewind_budget_mb = 256     # host memory the rewind history may hold
rewind_interval_frames = 25 # emulated frames per rewind step
run_ahead_frames = 0       # run-ahead input-latency reduction, 0..4 (0 = off)

The deterministic cycle-driven core is the only emulation timing. It is paced to wall-clock for the interactive window and runs unthrottled for headless captures; the emulated result is identical. (An older speed key here is accepted but ignored -- “real” was the only timing model, so it carried no information.)

  • power_on = false starts the machine powered off showing a test screen until you click the status-bar power button -- useful for arming video capture first. The power button cold-boots (reinitializing RAM according to [memory] init).

  • auto_launch = true makes the launcher run this configuration as soon as it opens it, including when it is loaded from the launcher. Set in the saved default configuration, it makes Copperline boot straight into the machine without showing the configuration screen. The launcher’s A/V & Emu -> Emulation -> Run on startup row controls this setting. Command-line launches are unaffected.

  • pacing_budget selects how real-time pacing budgets CPU work per frame: "cycles" (default) charges each instruction its actual 68000 cycle cost plus chip-bus waits, matching real hardware speed; "instructions" uses a flat COPPERLINE_REAL_CPU_CPI (default 4.0) cycles/instruction quota, which is cheaper but runs the CPU faster than hardware. COPPERLINE_REAL_PACING_BUDGET overrides this for one run. See The timing model for the full rationale.

  • realtime_priority = true asks the OS to schedule Copperline’s two latency-critical threads -- the wall-clock pacer and the audio callback -- above normal, which reduces frame stutter and audio glitches when the host is busy. It is best effort and off by default, and never fails the run:

    • macOS -- the pacer thread joins the USER_INTERACTIVE QoS class. The audio callback is left alone because Core Audio already runs it on a real-time thread (overriding that would only demote it).

    • Windows -- both threads are raised via SetThreadPriority; no privilege required.

    • Linux/other Unix -- raising priority needs privilege (an rtprio rlimit, CAP_SYS_NICE, or root). Without it the request is logged and declined, and the thread keeps normal scheduling.

    COPPERLINE_REALTIME_PRIORITY overrides this for one run; set it to 0/false/off to force it off, or to any other value (or leave it empty) to force it on.

  • warp_speed sets the default speed of Warp Speed (turbo) mode. With VSync enabled (the default), emulating one frame per presented frame would pin warp to the host monitor’s refresh rate. This option is an output frame skip -- "2x", "4x", "8x", "16x", or "max" (default) -- so warp retires that many emulated frames per presented frame, making warp roughly the limit times the refresh rate (host CPU permitting). "max" runs flat out and still presents at vsync when enabled. With VSync off, presentation frequency depends on host throughput. Adjust it live from the Warp Limit menu item or Cmd+Shift+W / Alt+Shift+W (see The window and its controls).

  • warp_boot = true accelerates boot sequences: from power-on, the machine runs unthrottled in warp mode (with audio muted) until storage activity (floppy and hard disk) remains idle for warp_boot_idle emulated seconds (default 10), at which point normal real-time execution and audio resume. Large setups such as AmigaVision or a full Workbench installation then reach their menus quickly. Set warp_boot_idle high enough to bridge expected pauses in disk access during boot (such as when SetPatch builds MMU tables across large memory configurations). CD audio playback does not count as storage activity, so a background CD-DA track cannot hold the warp phase open. If storage never becomes idle, warp boot times out after 600 emulated seconds. warp_until = SECS is the deterministic alternative: it warps until a fixed emulated timestamp. warp_boot and warp_until are mutually exclusive and cannot be combined with --run (which manages its own warp phase); --warp-boot and --warp-until set them from the command line. Toggling warp manually (Cmd+W / Alt+W) or sending warp.set {"on": false} over the control protocol ends the warp phase at once. Headless captures ignore these settings, since they run unthrottled anyway. The launcher’s Warp boot and Warp boot idle rows (A/V & Emu, Emulation) configure storage-idle mode, while a loaded warp_until setting appears as its own Until Ns option.

  • uaelib = true (default) enables the WinUAE-compatible service trap at $F0FF60. Guest programs can use this interface to toggle warp mode (via warpmode() in the vscode-amiga-debug template), emit debug log messages, and register bitmaps, palettes, and copper lists with the debugger (see Direct executable launching (--run)). It also enables the memory-write debug ports at $BFFF00 / $BFFF04. Setting this to false disables the ports and leaves $F0FF60 unmapped. On CDTV configurations, the extended ROM occupies $F00000 and covers the trap; the debug ports remain available.

  • uaelib_files = true lets the uaelib debug_load / debug_save calls read and write files below the --run program’s directory. It is off by default because guest programs may be untrusted; absolute paths, parent-directory traversal, and transfers over 16 MiB are always refused.

  • rewind = true records rewind history from power-on, so Cmd+Z / Alt+Z and the Rewind menu item can step the whole machine backward through it. It rides the same deterministic snapshot ring as the debugger’s reverse controls (see Reverse debugging) and is off by default because it is not free: rewind_budget_mb (default 256) of host memory holds the snapshots, and the whole machine is serialized once every rewind_interval_frames (default 25, half a second of PAL). One rewind step goes back exactly one interval; oldest snapshots are evicted first, so how much emulated time the budget buys scales with the machine’s RAM size. Turning the menu item off releases the retained snapshots. The same determinism preconditions as reverse debugging apply -- a real-time clock and host disk writes are not rolled back.

  • run_ahead_frames reduces input latency in compatible windowed sessions. Each refresh commits one ordinary frame, snapshots the machine, executes the requested number of future frames, presents the last future image, and restores the snapshot. Audio, serial output, and control events come only from the committed frame; speculative output is discarded. The committed machine timeline is therefore unchanged. This costs one whole-machine snapshot per refresh and roughly (run_ahead_frames + 1)x realtime host performance, so start at 1 and raise it only while the performance overlay shows comfortable headroom. Large values also skip visible intermediate animation.

    Run-ahead stays inactive when a speculative frame could observe or change host state that the snapshot cannot restore. This includes warp and headless capture, [cpu] speed = "fastest", RTG output, rewind/reverse debugging, debugger stops, injected faults, validation/SMC/heatmap/frame-analyzer observers, instruction or waveform traces, a connected control client, video recording, loaded save states, live serial or parallel devices, a video-slot card (Video Toaster), writable or physical floppy media, mounted CDs, hard-drive, PCMCIA, physical host-disk, and host-directory storage, host networking or plugin boards, MHI decoding, and a live or persistent RTC/NVRAM. Offline WAV and stem capture are supported: speculative audio is discarded at the mixer before any sink receives it. The Run Ahead item under Emulation Settings adjusts the level live and reports the current blocking reason. --run-ahead FRAMES overrides the config for one run.

[cpu]¶

[cpu]
model = "68000"     # 68000, 68010, 68EC020, 68020, 68EC030, 68030,
                    # 68EC040, 68040, 68EC060, 68060
clock_mhz = 14.0    # optional; defaults to the model's stock speed
# icache = false    # instruction-cache model (on by default on all 020+ models)
# dcache = false    # data-cache model (on by default: 030/040/060)
# fpu = true        # fit a 68881/68882 (needs the 68020+ coprocessor
#                   # interface, so not valid on a 68000/68010/68EC040/
#                   # 68EC060). The full 68040's and 68060's on-die FPUs
#                   # are on by default.
# unimplemented = "trap"  # 68040 and 68060 only: "trap" (faithful; the OS
#                   # needs 68040.library / 68060.library) or "native"
#                   # (execute the instructions left to software directly)
# jit = true        # experimental: fast batch/trace-JIT CPU execution
#                   # (68020+; not cycle-exact)
# speed = "fastest" # with jit: adapt the JIT clock to the host while the
#                   # window paces to real time, like WinUAE's "fastest
#                   # possible" (not reproducible; default "fixed")

  • model: the 68010 models the vector base register, the format-stacking exception model, and DBcc loop mode; the 68EC020 is a 68020 instruction set with a 24-bit external address bus. The 68EC030, 68EC040 and 68EC060 are their full parts without the paged MMU (the CPU in, for example, the A4000/030 and many budget accelerator boards): MMU register writes are taken without trapping wherever the silicon takes them, but no address is ever translated. They keep their caches, stock clock and 32-bit bus. The 68EC030’s access control unit takes the 68030’s MMU instructions without trapping: PMOVE reaches its AC0/AC1 and ACUSR registers, PTEST reports an AC0/AC1 match in ACUSR, and PFLUSH/PLOAD do nothing. It can still take a 68881/68882; the 68EC040 and 68EC060 have no FPU at all, so fpu = true is rejected for them. The FPU-less parts that keep the MMU (68LC040, 68LC060) are the 68040 and 68060 with fpu = false.

  • clock_mhz defaults to the model’s stock speed (68000/68010 ~7.09, 020 ~14, 030/040 ~25, 060 50) and is modelled as a whole multiple of the colour clock (3.546895 MHz), rounded to the nearest one. Fast RAM and ROM run at the CPU clock; chip and slow RAM stay chip-bus bound, so overclocking speeds up only what a real accelerator would speed up. The A1200 and CD32 profiles keep their authentic 14.18 MHz while [cpu] model is unset.

  • icache/dcache model the on-chip caches and default on for the silicon that has them (instruction cache on the 020/68EC020/030/040/060, data cache on the 030/040/060), matching real hardware where AmigaOS enables them via CACR. The cache is sized to the CPU: 256 bytes on the 020/030, 4 KB on the 040, 8 KB on the 060. This is not cosmetic: code that loops out of chip RAM otherwise contends with bitplane DMA on every instruction fetch and can run at roughly half speed, which is why an AGA demo’s music or animation may pace correctly only with the cache modelled. The data cache covers expansion RAM/ROM only, since chip and slow RAM are DMA-visible and cache-inhibited as on real Amigas. Set either key to false to opt out.

  • unimplemented (68040 and 68060 only) picks what happens on the instructions those chips leave to software. The 68060 dropped MOVEP, CHK2/CMP2, CAS2, misaligned CAS, 64-bit MUL/DIV, and most of the FPU beyond basic arithmetic (transcendentals, FMOVECR, packed decimal) from silicon. "trap" (the default) is what the chip does -- they raise the unimplemented-instruction exceptions and the OS-side 68060.library emulates them, as on a real CyberStorm or Blizzard board, so software using them needs that library installed. "native" executes them directly for systems without it. Kickstart 3.1 itself boots under "trap". On a 68040 with its FPU the same key covers what that FPU leaves to Motorola’s floating-point software package: the transcendental instructions, FMOD/FREM/FSCALE, FGETEXP/FGETMAN, FINT/FINTRZ, FMOVECR, packed decimal, and any denormalized or unnormalized operand of the instructions it does have. Under "trap" they take the Line-F and unsupported-data-type exceptions and 68040.library (loaded by SetPatch from LIBS:) emulates them from the FPU state frames, as on an A4000/040 or A3640; without the library the first such instruction ends in the OS’s exception handler, exactly as on the real machine. "native" computes them in the emulator instead. Kickstart 3.1 and the bundled AROS ROM boot under either setting; the 68EC040 and a 68040 with fpu = false have no FPU and are unaffected. The 68060’s FPU is not 68040-compatible (its FPU state frames are a different size from the ones Kickstart builds), so, as a real 060 board’s boot ROM does, Copperline disables it (PCR.DFP) on every reset and 68060.library enables it once it has adapted the OS. Without the library the system runs with no FPU under either setting. fpu = false on the 68060 models the LC060 (the 68EC060 is FPU-less too): its PCR identifies the FPU-less part ($0431) and keeps PCR.DFP set even when software clears it, so FP instructions always take the FPU-disabled exception. The 68060’s superscalar dual-issue and branch cache are modelled and activate when system software enables them (PCR.ESS and CACR.EBC, which 68060.library does at boot); until then the chip runs scalar, as on real silicon.

  • jit (experimental, also --jit/--no-jit) runs the CPU through the m68k core’s batch/trace-JIT path instead of the cycle-exact per-instruction model: hot code compiles to native traces, and fast RAM and ROM are read and written directly, with no bus cost. The machine behaves like an ideal accelerator running at clock_mhz: one instruction per CPU clock with zero-wait fast RAM and ROM, so a 50 MHz 68040 delivers on the order of 50 MIPS (raise clock_mhz for more). The boot ROMs of Copperline’s own [copperhf] and [[filesys]] boards count as ROM here, so their drivers run at CPU speed too. The CPU runs ahead of the chipset in batches that end at the next hardware event or chip-bus access, and interrupts are recognized only there, so chip-level races and cycle-counted effects no longer line up; leave it off for anything timing-sensitive (games, demos). Chip and slow RAM still arbitrate onto the shared chip bus in order, and the on-chip cache models stay active (as on a real accelerator, they are what lets chip-RAM-resident code run at CPU speed), so displays, blits, and device I/O work normally. Requires a 68020 or later: the 68000/68010 share one bus with the chipset and their floating-bus and prefetch semantics need the precise core, so jit = true on those models logs a note and stays precise (the launcher greys the toggle). Known issue: the bundled AROS ROM’s boot screen may stay grey under JIT on some 020+ configurations (the guest still runs; Kickstart ROMs are unaffected).

  • speed (also --cpu-speed) picks how fast the JIT runs. "fixed" (the default) runs it at clock_mhz, deterministically. "fastest" is the equivalent of WinUAE’s Fastest possible CPU setting: while the window paces the machine to real time, the chipset, audio and emulated time stay in real time, so the pointer and sound stay smooth, and the CPU gets the host time that is left. It uses that time in two ways:

    • The JIT’s clock adapts. It starts at clock_mhz, which is also its floor (it never runs slower), and rises while the host has headroom and the CPU is actually busy; a CPU waiting in STOP, or one stalled on the chip bus, keeps its clock. When the host gets loaded, for example by another program, the clock backs off toward clock_mhz again.

    • Before each frame is presented, the remaining host time runs extra CPU-only bursts. Code working in fast RAM and ROM runs there without advancing the chipset; a chip RAM or device access keeps its normal timing, and a short limit stops a polling loop from running the chipset through the whole interval.

    A chipset-heavy configuration can still run slower than real time on a slow host. The performance overlay (cpu N MHz) and the control protocol’s status reply (jit_mhz) show the measured throughput as an equivalent clock, bursts included, and the launcher’s CPU page has a matching JIT speed row, greyed until the JIT is on.

    The mode is deliberately not reproducible: how many instructions run per frame depends on the host and on what else it is doing, so two runs differ. Copperline logs this once at start. In detail:

    • It needs jit = true on a 68020 or later; any other combination is rejected with an error.

    • Runs without a wall clock -- --screenshot-after, --dump-frames, --gif-after, --expect-screenshot, --exit-on-return, --benchmark-until, headless --control and --gdb sessions -- have nothing to keep up with, so they stay at clock_mhz and match speed = "fixed" exactly. They remain deterministic; raise clock_mhz for a faster fixed CPU there. (COPPERLINE_HEADLESS_PACED=1 paces such a run like the window, and the clock then adapts as it would there; see Headless operation.)

    • Warp Speed runs the CPU at the last measured throughput as a fixed clock (never below clock_mhz); adaptation and the bursts resume when warp ends.

    • Netplay refuses it, and run-ahead stays inactive under it: both depend on re-running or comparing frames that must come out identical.

    • Save states do not store the adapted clock. A session whose clock has not adapted yet (any unpaced run) takes the loaded state’s CPU clock exactly, as speed = "fixed" does; one that has adapted keeps the clock it reached (never below the state’s clock_mhz). A resumed windowed run is not byte-identical to the original.

    • --record-input/--script replays, --expect-screenshot comparisons and reverse debugging are exact only in unpaced runs, where the clock is fixed.

    • Any debugger hook that forces the precise core (breakpoints, traces, COPPERLINE_DBG_*) suspends adaptation and the bursts, just as it suspends the JIT.

[memory]¶

[memory]
chip = "512K"        # OCS max 512K; ECS/AGA max 2M
fast = "0"           # Zorro II fast RAM at $200000: 64K..8M board sizes
slow = "512K"        # A500 trapdoor RAM at $C00000: 0 or up to 512K
init = "zero"        # or "random[:SEED]" / "pattern:0x5555" for read testing
motherboard = "0"    # Ramsey motherboard RAM (A3000/A4000): up to 16M (A4000: 64M)
accelerator = "0"    # CPU-slot RAM at $08000000 (32-bit CPUs): up to 128M
z3   = "0"           # Zorro III RAM (needs a 32-bit CPU): 64K..1G, power of two

Sizes take a K, M, or (for Zorro III) G suffix -- KB/KiB and so on work too -- or a plain byte count, and must be multiples of 4 KiB.

init controls cold power-on contents for writable system RAM. The default, "zero", preserves Copperline’s normal compatibility behaviour. "random" fills chip, slow, motherboard, accelerator, A1000 WCS, and RAM-backed Zorro boards with deterministic pseudo-random bytes, which helps expose guest code that reads memory before initializing it. The fixed default seed is identical across hosts and repeated cold resets; "random:SEED" selects another decimal or 0x hexadecimal 64-bit seed for test matrices. "pattern:WORD" instead repeats one decimal or 0x hexadecimal 16-bit word in big-endian Amiga byte order; for convenience a bare value such as "0x5555" means the same thing as "pattern:0x5555". The Machine Configuration screen exposes these as Power-on fill and Fill pattern on its Memory page. Warm keyboard resets still preserve RAM, and save-state restores reproduce the saved bytes exactly.

For a one-off developer run:

./target/release/copperline --ram-init random --config game.toml --noaudio \
  --screenshot-after 20 /tmp/game-random-ram.png

  • Chip RAM is range-checked against the chipset: 512K on OCS, 2M on ECS/AGA (also bounded by the selected Agnus revision’s address reach).

  • Fast RAM is exposed as a Zorro II autoconfig board at $200000, so it must be a legal Zorro II board size: 64K, 128K, 256K, 512K, 1M, 2M, 4M, or 8M. On the A600/A1200 more than 4M reaches the PCMCIA slot’s common-memory window at $600000 and disables the slot (see [pcmcia]).

  • Slow RAM ($C00000 “ranger” RAM) is arbitrated on the chip bus through Agnus exactly like chip RAM -- it is slow in the authentic way.

  • Motherboard RAM is the 32-bit local memory Ramsey drives on the A3000/A4000: it ends at $08000000 and grows downward (16M reaches $07000000), and Kickstart sizes it with its own probe -- no autoconfig involved. It needs a Ramsey ([machine] mem_controller, fitted by the A3000/A4000 profiles, which also fit their stock 4M of this RAM by default) and a 32-bit CPU, and must fill whole Ramsey banks: 1M-4M in 1M steps, or 8M, 12M, 16M. On the A4000 (Ramsey-07), sizes beyond 16M keep growing downward into the $04000000-$06FFFFFF motherboard RAM expansion space, in 4M steps up to 64M (which reaches $04000000). Set motherboard = "0" to remove it.

  • Accelerator RAM is CPU-slot local memory: it starts at $08000000 and grows upward through the coprocessor-slot expansion space, up to 128M (ending at $10000000, where Zorro III space begins). This is the RAM an accelerator/CPU board carries, so it needs a 32-bit CPU but no particular machine profile; any whole number of megabytes fits. Kickstart sizes it with its own probe, like the motherboard bank.

  • Z3 RAM requires a 68020/68030/68040/68060 (a 24-bit bus cannot reach it); Kickstart assigns its base address, usually $40000000.

Additional expansion boards can be described with [[zorro]] metadata files; see Writing Zorro board plugins.

[chipset]¶

[chipset]
revision = "OCS"   # OCS, ECS, or AGA preset
video = "PAL"      # PAL or NTSC
# agnus = "8372A"  # optional fine-grained override
# denise = "OCS"   # optional fine-grained override
# genlock = true   # an external genlock supplies sync (default false)

revision is a preset; agnus and denise allow the mixed configurations real machines shipped with (a late A500 with an ECS Agnus but OCS Denise, for example):

  • agnus: OCS/8370/8371 (OCS), 8372/8372A (ECS, 1M chip), 8375/8372B (ECS, 2M chip), 8374/ALICE (AGA).

  • denise: OCS/8362, ECS/8373, LISA/4203.

The ECS preset picks an 8372A for up to 1M chip RAM and an 8375 above; the A500Plus and A600 profiles always use the 8375, as the real boards did, and the A500 and A2000 profiles the 8372A with the OCS Denise until a revision says otherwise. The AGA preset resolves to Alice and Lisa: 8 bitplanes, the 256-entry 25-bit palette with BPLCON3 BANK/LOCT banking, HAM8, FMODE wide bitplane and sprite fetch (DMA and manual sprites), SSCAN2/BSCAN2 scan doubling, 35 ns BPLCON3 SPRES output, BPLCON4, and CLXCON2. Remaining gaps are recorded in Chipset modules.

genlock = true fits an external genlock supplying sync. Setting BPLCON0.ERSY then slaves the beam to that sync instead of stopping it, so the beam counters (VPOSR/VHPOSR) keep moving; the external sync runs at the machine’s own timing. Without a genlock, ERSY freezes the counters, as on a real Amiga with nothing in the genlock socket. Software written for a genlock or a video-slot card that supplies sync (the NewTek Video Toaster) runs with ERSY set and waits on the beam, so it needs this. Kickstart’s genlock probe also finds the genlock, so the OS hides the programmable 31 kHz modes that a genlock cannot follow. A video-slot card that supplies its own sync sets this for as long as it is fitted.

[video_slot]¶

[video_slot]
card = "toaster"          # "none" (default) or "toaster"
media = "C:/Toaster/Amiga Toaster Files"   # the card's host folder
# monitors = true         # Preview and Program monitor windows (default true)
# preview_overlay = false # the switcher interface over Preview (default false)
# volume = "ToasterFiles"  # also mount media in the Amiga as ToasterFiles:
# flyer = false           # also fit a Video Flyer (needs card = "toaster")
# converter = true        # with a Flyer, open the clip converter window too

card = "toaster" fits an emulated NewTek Video Toaster 4000 in the A4000’s video slot: a card that watches the digital RGB output line by line and answers on the parallel port, as the real one does. The NewTek switcher (Toaster 4.x) then starts, passes its own card tests and runs; the Toaster software and the Kickstart ROM are not included and must be supplied. The card supplies genlock sync while fitted (see [chipset] genlock).

media is the folder that stands in for the card’s connectors (default: Amiga Toaster Files in Copperline’s own folder). It is created with these subfolders on first use:

  • Input 1 .. Input 4: what is plugged into each video input. Drop video files or still pictures in; several play one after another in name order and loop (a still among several shows for five emulated seconds), and an empty folder is an unplugged input. Changes are picked up while the machine runs. A file plays in emulated time: the machine waits for the decoder, so the same files give the same output on a fast or a slow host, headless or windowed. Stills (PNG, JPEG, BMP) need nothing else; video files are decoded by ffmpeg: the program the COPPERLINE_FFMPEG environment variable names, else ffmpeg.exe (or ffmpeg) in the folder itself, beside Copperline, on the PATH, or in the usual package-manager folders (see MP4 recordings).

  • Output: recordings of the Program output (MP4 or AVI, see below).

  • Flyer: the Video Flyer’s drives, Flyer/FA0 and so on (see flyer below).

A video file’s sound comes along with its picture and follows the switcher: what is on Program is what you hear, through the emulator’s sound output, mixed by how much of each input Program shows (a dissolve crossfades the sound, a wipe by area, framestores and mattes are silent). Recordings carry the same sound. The real card handles picture only; this stands in for the audio-follow-video mixer beside it.

Until the switcher first drives the card, while the machine boots, both outputs are black and silent and the input folders are not read yet; the inputs start playing once the switcher is up.

The switcher’s own screen is an NTSC overscan display, taller and wider than the standard TV picture, so the default TV framing leaves its bottom rows (the AUTO/TAKE row and the version line) and its left edge off the glass. [display] overscan = "smart" with autocrop = true crops the window to the display window the switcher programs instead, which shows the whole screen; Video Settings -> Framing and Autocrop in the menu switch the same settings live.

With monitors on, the card’s two outputs open as windows of their own, each on a picture monitor: Preview and Program. Closing one only hides it; Recording -> Show Toaster Monitors brings both back.

The monitors’ front-panel buttons work, as on a studio monitor:

  • POWER switches the tube on or off. Switched on (and when the windows open), the degaussing coil thumps and hums and the picture comes up as the tube warms; switched off, the picture collapses to a line, then a dot that fades. The sounds are made by Copperline and played on the host’s output only: they are not part of the machine’s sound, its WAV capture or a recording. A recording carries on with the monitor off.

  • APERTURE, BRIGHT, CHROMA, PHASE and CONTRAST (up on the top row, down below; hold to repeat) adjust the picture on the monitor only: peaking, black level, saturation, hue and gain. The level shows on the screen for a moment. RESET puts them back to their presets, which leave the picture exactly as the card made it (the lamp above RESET is lit at the presets).

  • VOL on the Program monitor is the level of the card’s sound on the host’s speakers (switched off, the Program monitor is silent); recordings keep the sound as made. On the Preview monitor it only shows its level.

  • BLUE ONLY drives the blue gun alone, UNDER SCAN shows the whole raster inside the glass, and H-V DELAY shows the blanking and sync across the middle of the picture. INPUT B and C select inputs with nothing connected (a dark screen; A is the card). ANALOG/DIGITAL only lights.

The settings are kept per monitor in the media folder’s .copperline/monitors.json.

In the Program window, the REC button on the monitor’s top edge (or R) starts and stops recording the Program output, picture and sound, into Output (its lamp lights red while it runs); Recording -> Record Toaster Program does the same. SETUP beside it opens the recording setup over the picture: the format, MP4 (H.264 video with square pixels and AAC sound; the default) or the recorder’s lossless AVI, the MP4’s quality (Standard, CRF 18 and 192 kb/s, or High, CRF 12 and 320 kb/s), and a button that opens the Output folder. An MP4 is recorded into an AVI beside it first and made from it with ffmpeg when the recording stops (the button reads SAVING and the title says so until it is done; the AVI is then removed, or kept if ffmpeg is missing or fails). The setup is kept in the media folder’s .copperline/recording.json. The monitor artwork can be replaced by a monitor-program.png or monitor-preview.png in the media folder (or monitor.png for both): the tube is found as the area around the picture’s centre enclosed by a near-black gap. A replaced artwork has no working front panel.

Effect sounds. Some transitions carry sounds (8SVX samples in the effect, such as Shatter, Falling Sheep or Camera Iris) that the switcher plays through the Amiga’s own audio, which Copperline mixes into its sound output and the recordings. NewTek’s switcher skips them when a Flyer is fitted (animfxhandler.a: “dont do sound if flyer!”), so with flyer = true they are silent, as they were on a real Toaster-Flyer; without the Flyer they play.

volume also mounts the media folder in the Amiga as a volume of that name (like a [[filesys]] entry, never a boot candidate), so the Toaster software can load framestores from the input folders and save into Output, and so the control link below can reach the Amiga. The usual name is ToasterFiles.

Control link. With volume set and S:Copperline-Link.rexx (from Copperline’s assets/toaster) started by S:User-Startup (Run >NIL: SYS:Rexxc/RX S:Copperline-Link.rexx), an MCP client can drive the Toaster software itself: the bridge drops ARexx jobs into the media folder’s .copperline subfolder and the script runs them inside the Amiga (see MCP server in the control-protocol reference: tools toaster_switcher, toaster_project, toaster_program, toaster_rexx, next to toaster_status, toaster_capture, toaster_record, toaster_input, and the Flyer clip tools flyer_import, flyer_export, flyer_list). A job puts the switcher’s and the editor’s ARexx hosts on ARexx’s shared list of function hosts only while it runs: left there (an addlib with no remlib, in any script), they take the calls of the CG’s own macros and hang them.

Assigns. The Toaster software expects what NewTek’s installer adds to S:User-Startup: Assign Toaster: on the NewTek folder, Assign REXX: Toaster:Arexx ADD (the CG runs its start-up macro, which loads the fonts it starts with, and its Alt-F keys from REXX:CG), Assign HIIP: Toaster:Programs/Hiip_Support (the image loaders and savers) and, for ToasterPaint and older CG pages, Assign ToasterFonts: Toaster:PSFonts.

Flyer clips. The flyerclip program (built from source and Homebrew with Copperline) converts between video files and NewTek Video Flyer clips, the Flyer’s own format: VTASC-coded NTSC composite fields and 16-bit stereo sound (crates/flyerclip, transcribed from NewTek’s Flyer sources; the format is written up in crates/flyerclip/FORMAT.md). flyerclip import movie.mp4 writes movie.clip onto the Flyer’s first drive, the media folder’s Flyer/FA0 folder; flyerclip export movie.clip writes movie.mp4 beside it; flyerclip info describes a clip. Dropping a file on the program does the right one. --hq5/--hq6 give each field a larger budget, --no-audio drops the sound and --seconds N stops early. ffmpeg does the decoding and encoding.

How a source becomes a clip: ffmpeg squares its pixels first (anamorphic video keeps its shape), fits it to 4:3 (letterboxed or pillarboxed, like a Toaster input, unless the converter below says crop or stretch) and scales it to the Flyer’s 752 samples by 480 lines. Each field is its own moment, 59.94 a second, as a camera records: an interlaced source is split into its fields, a progressive one sampled at the field rate (24 frame film comes out with 3:2 pulldown, 60 frame video keeps every frame), and the four fields of each colour frame take the lines of four pictures in turn. The sound is resampled to the Flyer’s 44.056 kHz.

The clip converter. flyer-convert (built from source and Homebrew with Copperline; invoked standalone as flyer-convert [--media DIR] [FILE|FOLDER...]) is the same conversion in a window of its own, drawn in the Toaster’s style. With a Flyer fitted, a windowed Copperline starts it beside the machine, pointed at media (converter = false stops that); it runs on its own, can stay open after the machine quits, and a second copy started while one runs just exits. Drop video files, still pictures, folders or a folder of numbered pictures (one sequence) on it, or use Add Files / Add Folder; choose the Flyer drive, quality (Standard, HQ5, HQ6), motion (fields at 59.94 or frames at 29.97), the fit, how long stills last and how fast a sequence plays, the sound (stereo, mono or none) and its gain per channel, and Convert. Each clip lands on the drive with its crouton icon (<clip>.I, a frame a second in), so the Grazer shows it with a picture straight away; a .clip file dropped on it is copied over as it is. The preview shows the selected source as the clip will carry it, fitted, and follows the conversion while it runs. Its settings are kept in flyer-convert.json beside the program.

Video Flyer. flyer = true (with card = "toaster") also fits a NewTek Video Toaster Flyer, the Zorro II card that records and plays clips into the Toaster’s inputs 3 and 4. The Toaster software finds it as NewTek’s board (manufacturer 2191, product 0) and loads it as on a real machine: FlyerInit (or the switcher at start-up) downloads the Flyer’s firmware and chip files from NewTek:Programs/Flyer_Support and reports “Okay”, and the switcher then starts with its Flyer controls. The card’s own processor is not emulated: the window is its shared memory, and the commands the software leaves there are answered by Copperline as the Flyer’s firmware would (the board’s serial number is in the 2CC range of the installed chipset.dat; its EEPROM settings last until the emulator quits). COPPERLINE_DIAG_FLYER=1 logs every command it is sent.

The Flyer’s SCSI drives are folders in media’s Flyer folder: FA0 (bus A, unit 0; created when missing), and FB0, FC0, ... when those folders exist. Files are the clips’ bytes as the Flyer stores them (what flyerclip import and the converter write, or a clip copied off a real Flyer drive); a .flyervol file whose first line is a name renames the volume, which is otherwise FlyerA0, FlyerB0, ... With the Toaster’s FA0 DOS driver mounted (copy NewTek/Programs/System_Support/Devs/DOSDrivers/FA0 into DEVS:DOSDrivers), the drive is the FlyerA0: volume, which lists, reads and copies like any other. Clips are read-only (they cannot be overwritten, extended or deleted from the Amiga, and nothing records into the drives yet, though Process Clip below makes new ones from them); other files, such as the crouton icons below, are written straight into the folder. A name the Amiga gives a new or renamed file or drawer must be one ordinary host file name: one that starts with a dot or holds a backslash is refused (as is a DOS device name such as NUL on a Windows host), so nothing is written outside the drive’s folder or hidden from its own listing. Clips put into the folder while the machine runs show up the next time the Grazer lists the drive.

A typical start-up, as in the Toaster’s own installation: S:Toaster-Auto (or S:User-Startup) runs NewTek:Programs/System_Support/c/FlyerInit before rx Toaster:Programs/StartToaster, so the Flyer is set up when the switcher starts.

Playing clips. Clips go into a project like any crouton: from the Grazer (the FlyerA0: drive), or with the Editor’s ARexx CROUTONLOAD('FlyerA0:movie.clip'). A clip’s crouton shows a picture from the clip once it has an icon: the Editor’s MAKEICON('FlyerA0:movie.clip', field) (or the Flyer controls) has the switcher read that field off the drive and write movie.clip.I beside the clip, as on a real Flyer. Playing the project (or PROJECTPLAY) hands the clips to the Flyer as a sequence; the Flyer plays them at the right fields on its channels A and B, which take over the Toaster’s inputs 3 and 4 while it plays (the switcher routes them with the Flyer’s ToasterMux), so the project’s transitions run between the clips as on the real system. A clip crouton run on its own (CROUTONRUN, or from the switcher) plays the same way; CROUTONSTOP stops it. In/out points, audio volume, pan, attack and decay and audio envelopes come from the croutons’ settings, as the Editor sends them.

The Flyer’s sound is the system’s sound: its eight-channel mixer’s output (735 samples a field, about 44.056 kHz, locked to the video) goes to the emulator’s sound output and into the Program recording, whatever the switcher shows. The input folders’ sound keeps following Program as described above (it stands in for what would reach the Flyer’s line inputs); an input the Flyer has taken over is silent there.

Jog and shuttle work as on the real card: opening a clip’s controls puts the clip on Program (through input 3 or 4), and dragging its in/out sliders, jogging with the mouse or the arrow keys (Shift for 30 frames), or holding a shuttle arrow moves the picture through the clip a colour frame at a time, with the sound of each frame heard as it goes. While the position stands still the frame’s sound repeats as a short loop, as on the real Flyer, until the next move or until the controls close (the Editor’s own quieting after a pause does not happen yet). The shuttle moves at the speeds the switcher asks for rather than racing to the end.

Process Clip (the cutting room) works: mark the pieces of a clip with their in and out points and names, choose picture, sound or both, and Perform makes each piece a clip of its own on the drive, copied from the original’s coded frames (whole colour frames, so a piece starts on the colour frame holding its in point), with its icon. Without Destructive the original stays. A destructive cut takes the original off the drive as the Flyer would, but its file is moved into a Trash folder beside the drive folders rather than deleted, so it can be put back. Not emulated yet: recording into the Flyer, SMPTE time code and the TBC module.

Flyer clips are decoded ahead of time on worker threads (two to four), so playback does not hold up the emulated machine; the picture is the same whatever the host’s speed. [cpu] jit = true runs the switcher, the Editor and Flyer playback correctly but does not make them faster: while a project plays, the switcher’s time goes on chip-bus and CIA accesses, which the JIT runs at the same speed as the precise core.

preview_overlay lets the switcher draw its interface over the Preview output when its own preference asks for it, as a one-monitor Toaster setup does. It is off by default because the interface has a window of its own.

Headless screenshots (--screenshot-after) also save each output on its monitor beside the capture (shot-preview.png, shot-program.png). COPPERLINE_DIAG_TOASTER=1 logs what the card decodes and the bus state it outputs; =fields also dumps one field’s line headers in forty; =perf logs, once an emulated second, the host time each stage of the card’s work took (toaster perf: lines: painting the field, scanning its headers, each source, the key, the mix, publishing, the Flyer’s decodes and waits), most of it on the card’s own compose thread, with submit and compose_wait the emulation thread’s share. How the card works is described in The video pipeline and in src/toaster/.

[display]¶

[display]
overscan = "tv"       # "tv" (default), "smart" or "full"
tv_h_centre = 0       # TV picture centring in lo-res pixels, -16..16 (+ = right)
tv_v_centre = 0       # TV picture centring in scan lines, -8..8 (+ = down)
pixel_aspect = "tv"   # "tv" (default, 4:3 CRT) or "square" (exact 2x2 lo-res)
scaling = "smooth"    # "smooth" (default, aspect fit) or "integer" (whole multiples)
autocrop = false      # crop the window to the programmed display window (default false)
deinterlace = true    # motion-adaptive interlace weaving (default true)
phosphor = 0.0        # CRT persistence fraction, 0.0 (off) to 0.95
shader = "none"       # "none" (default), "scanlines", "mask", "crt", or a .wgsl file
shader_strength = 1.0 # how strongly the shader is mixed in, 0.0-1.0
bezel = "off"         # monitor front: "off" (default), "1084", or "classic"
# bezel_stickers = "stickers"  # folder of PNG stickers for the bezel (default: none)
perf_overlay = false  # show the performance overlay at start (default false)
tint = "none"         # "none" (default), "bw", "green", "amber", or "sepia"
menu_scale = "1x"     # size of the pop-up menu: "1x" (default) or "2x"
full_screen = false   # open borderless fullscreen at start (default false)
maximized = false     # maximize with title bar and desktop taskbar (default false)
monitor = "auto"      # host display: auto, primary, one-based number, or exact name
# position = [100, 80] # window top-left in logical pixels relative to monitor
window_scale = 1.0    # initial window width and height multiplier, 0.5-4.0
# title = "{app} {version} · {machine} · {rom}"
status_bar = true     # show the status bar at start (default true)
track_display = "track"  # floppy counter: "track" (default) or "cylinder" (CYL.SIDE)
vsync = true          # synchronize desktop presentation to vblank (default true)
hidpi_texture = true  # draw the presentation texture at device-pixel density (default true)

The default window title shows the machine and boot ROM. For a different layout, set title with {app}, {version}, {machine} (or {m}), {rom} (or {r}), and {hash} (eight hexadecimal digits of the loaded ROM). Other text is literal; {{ and }} insert braces. For example, title = "Workbench test · {m} · {r}" gives an instance a visible name. Known Kickstarts use their checksum-identified version; AROS and unrecognized ROMs include the short hash. The title follows ROM changes and loaded states.

vsync controls desktop presentation. On uses strict FIFO vsync to prevent tearing. Off requests unsynchronized presentation where the graphics backend supports it; it may reduce latency but can tear. Video Settings -> VSync changes it live without restarting or changing normal emulation speed. The choice carries into the configuration screen when saving a config. Headless captures and the browser frontend are unaffected. Roughly 50 Hz PAL output can still show an uneven cadence on fixed 60 Hz or 120 Hz displays: VSync does not make those refresh rates match.

hidpi_texture decides the resolution of the texture the window is drawn from. On (the default) it follows the display’s device-pixel density, so a 200% (Retina) window is fed a 2x texture and every host row picks its own woven scanline. Off keeps the texture at canvas resolution and leaves the upscale to the GPU’s scaler pass, a quarter of the per-frame texture upload (and of the CPU copy, when a menu or overlay makes the frame compose on the CPU) -- worth trying on a slow host that falls short of real time in a high-density window. Integer scaling looks the same either way (its whole-number blocks are point-sampled from the 1x texture); the smooth fit selects rows at canvas resolution instead of the finer texture grid, which fine interlaced detail can show. Captures are never affected.

The emulated framebuffer always carries the full overscan field Denise produces; overscan picks how much of it is presented. "tv" presents what the monitor’s glass shows: the captured aperture -- the standard window plus the symmetric overscan margin the framebuffer captures on its right edge -- fills the whole 4:3 glass, the way a real set’s raster overscans its screen, so the picture (border colour included) reaches every edge with no black bezel columns. The live window and PNG screenshots / --dump-frames present the same 716x540 glass. PAL and NTSC scans share that shape because both apertures fill the same glass: an NTSC scan’s shorter crop (the 200-line standard window plus the same overscan margin) is scaled onto the same output rows. "full" shows everything, which is useful when debugging display alignment. COPPERLINE_OVERSCAN=full|tv|smart overrides this for a single run. In all modes the presentation geometry holds steady across the blank frames a screen change produces: a frame showing only border colour keeps the previous frame’s aperture and centring instead of snapping to the full framebuffer, so the picture does not jump sideways at Kickstart screen changes.

"smart" keeps the TV aperture and automatically adjusts its horizontal position after the hardware display envelope has remained stable for 25 distinct presented emulated frames. The automatic correction is limited to eight lo-res pixels each way; blank frames retain the last position, and small display windows do not pull the aperture toward individual objects. It can bring slightly off-centre artwork, such as the CD32 boot logo, into view without zooming out. Manual H/V centring remains available as a trim; the combined horizontal correction is limited to the manual control’s 16-pixel travel. The menu’s Video Settings -> Framing switches between TV, Smart and Full overscan live. TV remains the default.

Smart framing follows display geometry, not software identity or pixel colour. A fixed aperture can still crop a large overscan display, and deliberate effects in its newly exposed margin may become visible. Use TV for a fixed crop, or Full overscan to inspect the entire captured field.

tv_h_centre / tv_v_centre nudge where the TV presentation centres the picture on the glass -- the H-CENTER/V-CENTER controls a real monitor carried on its front. tv_h_centre is in lo-res pixels, positive moving the picture right; tv_v_centre in scan lines, positive moving it down. The default aperture centres the standard window, which leaves most of the captured left overscan off-glass; software that leans its artwork into that overscan (the CD32 boot logo’s leading “A” serif, for example) comes fully into view a few pixels of tv_h_centre later, as it did on a set whose picture sat a little right of centre. Glass the nudge exposes beyond the captured raster is unscanned and shows black. The knobs move the TV aperture, so overscan = "full" ignores them; captures (screenshots, frame dumps) follow them like the live window. The menu’s Screen Centring rows (under Video Settings) step the same knobs live; the change is remembered like any menu setting.

pixel_aspect selects how emulated scanlines map to host rows. The default "tv" presents the field with the non-square pixel aspect of a 4:3 CRT: the full overscan scan fills a 4:3 picture, so PAL lo-res pixels come out slightly wider than tall, as a real TV shows them (a 320x256 screen spans about 640x482 window pixels). "square" uses one host row per woven scanline instead, so every low-resolution pixel is an integer 2x2 square and a 320x256 PAL screen occupies precisely 640x512 window pixels -- slightly taller than a real CRT picture, but exact for side-by-side pixel comparison with square-pixel emulators. The menu’s Pixel Aspect item flips the mode live (remembered like any menu setting), and COPPERLINE_PIXEL_ASPECT=tv|square overrides it for a single run.

scaling selects how that presentation canvas reaches the window, which is a separate question from what the canvas is. The default "smooth" fits the canvas to the window preserving its aspect ratio and interpolates, so the picture always uses the full window height (or width) whatever fraction the scale works out to. "integer" instead draws the canvas at whole-number multiples -- the largest that fits the window, measured in physical device pixels, and under the TV aspect a separate whole number per axis (below) -- centred in black borders and point-sampled: every canvas pixel becomes the same block of host pixels, with no row or column sampled twice, which is the look WinUAE and Amiberry call integer scaling.

The fit is taken in whole canvas pixels against the physical surface: the canvas is re-rendered at whatever factor fits, rather than drawn at whole multiples of a fixed high-DPI texture, so every step exists on every display. A 2x-DPI laptop whose screen holds three physical pixels per canvas pixel but not four gets the 3x picture, and fractional desktop scales such as 150% take their whole physical multiples the same way. A 5K or 6K display in fullscreen fills as much of its height as the next whole multiple allows. The internal render factor is capped at 4x but the displayed multiple is not, so the display’s pixels stay exact whole blocks past the cap; only the status bar and menus, drawn at the capped factor, are resampled there. Only when the window is too small for even a 1:1 copy -- smaller than the canvas itself in physical pixels -- does the picture fall back to the smooth fit rather than cropping to what fits. RTG board modes follow the setting too: their frame is scaled from its own native resolution, so a 640x480 board screen is drawn at 1x, 2x, 3x of those pixels inside the display area. The fit uses the window area above the status bar and open panel strips, independently of the chipset canvas: a 640x480 board screen fits at 2x on a 1920x1080 display. The debugger’s display pane uses the same native fit. The performance readout, the on-screen messages and the recording badge sit at the corners of that picture. Menus, panels and their translucent backgrounds use the same brightness as chipset displays. Menus and panels keep the UI canvas’s proportions and scale, independently of the board mode. They are composited over the native RTG texture, so opening them preserves its exact pixel blocks, size and position, including with the status bar hidden.

Integer scaling draws from the unresampled canvas (one host row per woven scanline, matching pixel_aspect = "square"). Under the default TV aspect, the horizontal and vertical axes take independent integer multiples to approximate the 4:3 CRT pixel aspect (PAL pixels about 1.08x wider than tall, NTSC about 0.85x). The scaler picks the tallest integer fit whose aspect is within 10% of the display shape. With autocrop freeing the vertical margin that unused borders take, NTSC 200-line games reach a 4:5 pixel aspect on a 1080p display (a 1280x1000 active area), 6:7 at 1440p, and 4:5 at 4K. PAL uses square integer multiples until the display is tall enough for an 8:7 ratio. Odd scanline multiples stay crisp on progressive displays because woven line pairs are identical. pixel_aspect = "square" with "integer" keeps the multiples uniform and square, for side-by-side pixel comparisons. Switching integer scaling on in TV mode resizes the window to the unresampled canvas; interactive screenshots follow it, while scheduled captures keep the configured aspect geometry. Monitor bezels (bezel) use the resampled TV canvas under both scaling modes. Programmable (ECS/AGA VARBEAMEN) and RTG displays scale by uniform integer multiples. The menu’s Video Settings -> Scaling item switches modes at runtime.

autocrop (default off) crops the window display to the active raster window the hardware programs rather than showing the entire TV aperture. Most software occupies less than the full raster (a 320x200 screen, for example, uses 400 of 570 PAL woven lines), so cropping the unused borders lets the active image fill more of a 16:9 or 21:9 monitor. With scaling = "integer", the integer multiple is recalculated for the cropped dimensions, which often allows a larger factor.

The crop area is computed dynamically each frame from scanlines containing fetched bitplane data. The viewport expands immediately when a program opens a larger display and tightens smoothly after a smaller viewport has remained stable for roughly half a second, preventing visual jitter during scene changes. The status bar and overlay panels remain docked at the bottom of the window; opening a menu or panel temporarily reveals the full display area so no controls are obscured. Interactive screenshots follow the visible crop. Scheduled screenshots, frame dumps, and recordings capture the full configured aperture. CRT shader presets render over the cropped area. Programmable multisync modes (such as DblPAL or 31 kHz displays) are also cropped based on their active display windows. Autocrop is automatically suspended when using monitor bezels or RTG modes. The menu’s Video Settings -> Autocrop option toggles it at runtime.

For an automatic crop with the largest integer fit, use:

[display]
overscan = "smart"
autocrop = true
scaling = "integer"

Smart autocrop selects directly from the unmasked raster, before the TV aperture clips its edges. It includes the full detected display window, including artwork outside the usual TV view. PAL/NTSC pixel aspect comes from the scan rather than from the crop dimensions. For a 320x200 display on a 1920x1080 surface with the status bar hidden, PAL fits at 5x; NTSC uses the existing per-axis 4:5 fit. Larger title screens reduce the scale to fit their complete detected display. No picture lines are discarded to reach a larger multiplier. The detector uses fetched raster lines and programmed display spans; black pixels inside those spans remain picture content. This is automatic framing rather than per-game overscaling presets. Captures retain the configured aperture and centring, as with ordinary autocrop. Monitor bezels and RTG modes suspend autocrop.
